lesson.calculation: The calculation of the selected cell
lesson.entered: {cell} is part of the data you entered. Nothing was calculated here; the next steps start from these values.

decision.title: The decision
decision.idea: Everything starts from the table of alternatives and criteria, and from the weight of each criterion.
decision.why: Each criterion is either a benefit (higher is better) or a cost (lower is better). The weights say how much each criterion counts: the larger the weight, the more it moves the result.

reference.title: Best and worst
reference.idea: Two imaginary alternatives are added: one with the best value of every criterion (ideal) and one with the worst (anti-ideal).
reference.why: MARCOS judges every alternative by comparing it with these two reference rows. For a benefit criterion the best value is the largest; for a cost criterion it is the smallest.

normalize.title: Compare with the best
normalize.idea: Every value is compared with the best value of its criterion.
normalize.why: Criteria have different units, such as money, hours and points, which cannot be added up. After this step every value lies between 0 and 1, and 1 always means as good as the best.

weigh.title: Weigh and add up
weigh.idea: Each 0–1 value is multiplied by the weight of its criterion, and the results of a row are added up.
weigh.why: This way important criteria count for more. The sum S of a row is the overall performance of that alternative; the ideal row has the largest possible sum.

degrees.title: Compare with both references
degrees.idea: Each sum is divided by the sum of the anti-ideal row (K⁻) and by the sum of the ideal row (K⁺).
degrees.why: K⁻ shows how far an alternative is above the worst, K⁺ how close it comes to the best. MARCOS uses both to find a balanced score.

utility.title: One final score
utility.idea: The two degrees are combined into utility functions and then into one final utility f(K).
utility.why: The final utility is a compromise between being close to the ideal and far from the anti-ideal. The higher it is, the better the alternative.

ranking.title: Why this order?
ranking.idea: The alternatives are ordered by their final utility, highest first.
ranking.why: Below: the winner, the criteria that carried it, and where the runner-up is ahead or behind.

normalized-weight.how: The weight of {cell} is divided by the sum of all weights.
normalized-weight.meaning: {value} of the total weight goes to {cell}. The normalized weights add up to 1.

anti-ideal-benefit.how: {column} is a benefit criterion (higher is better), so its worst value is the smallest one in the column. It goes into the anti-ideal row.
anti-ideal-benefit.meaning: {value} is the lowest value any alternative has on {column}. No alternative does worse.

anti-ideal-cost.how: {column} is a cost criterion (lower is better), so its worst value is the largest one in the column. It goes into the anti-ideal row.
anti-ideal-cost.meaning: {value} is the highest, and so the worst, value on {column}.

ideal-benefit.how: For the benefit criterion {column} the best value is the largest one in the column. It goes into the ideal row.
ideal-benefit.meaning: {value} is the target on {column}: in the next step every alternative is measured against it.

ideal-cost.how: For the cost criterion {column} the best value is the smallest one in the column. It goes into the ideal row.
ideal-cost.meaning: {value} is the target on {column}: in the next step every alternative is measured against it.

benefit.how: {column} is a benefit criterion: the value of {row} is divided by the best (ideal) value of the column.
benefit.meaning: On {column}, {row} reaches {value} of the best value. 1 would mean it is the best.

cost.how: {column} is a cost criterion, so the division is turned around: the best (smallest) value is divided by the value of {row}.
cost.meaning: On {column}, {row} scores {value}. The lower the cost, the closer the result is to 1, and 1 is the best.

weighted.how: The 0–1 value of {row} on {column} is multiplied by the weight of {column}.
weighted.meaning: {value} is what {column} contributes to the score of {row}. A heavier criterion contributes more.

sum.how: The weighted values in the row of {cell} are added up.
sum.meaning: {value} is the overall performance S of {cell}. The ideal row has the largest possible sum.

k-minus.how: The sum of {row} is divided by the sum of the anti-ideal row.
k-minus.meaning: {row} performs {value} times as well as the worst possible alternative. Larger is better.

k-plus.how: The sum of {row} is divided by the sum of the ideal row.
k-plus.meaning: {row} reaches {value} of the ideal. 1 would mean it is as good as the ideal on every criterion.

f-k-minus.how: The utility with respect to the anti-ideal: K⁺ divided by K⁺ + K⁻. Note the crossover: K⁺ is in the numerator, as the authors define it.
f-k-minus.meaning: {value} is the share of K⁺ in K⁺ + K⁻. Because K⁻ and K⁺ are both proportional to S, it is the same for every alternative.

f-k-plus.how: The utility with respect to the ideal: K⁻ divided by K⁺ + K⁻.
f-k-plus.meaning: {value} is the share of K⁻ in K⁺ + K⁻. It is also the same for every alternative.

final-utility.how: K⁺ and K⁻ of {cell} are added up and divided by a term made from the two utility functions.
final-utility.meaning: {value} is the final utility of {cell}. The alternative with the highest value ranks first.

decision.title: The decision
decision.idea: Everything starts from ratings as triangular fuzzy numbers (l, m, u), and from the weight of each criterion.
decision.why: A fuzzy value says: between l and u, most likely m. Ratings given in words, such as good or poor, become such triangles through a linguistic scale. The weights say how much each criterion counts.

reference.title: Best and worst
reference.idea: The ideal and anti-ideal rows take the best and the worst l, m and u of every criterion.
reference.why: As in MARCOS, every alternative is compared with these two rows. Each of the three numbers of a triangle is handled on its own.

normalize.title: Compare with the best
normalize.idea: Every triangle is divided by one number of the ideal: its u for a benefit criterion, its l for a cost criterion.
normalize.why: This brings every criterion to a common scale between 0 and 1, and the three numbers stay in order, l ≤ m ≤ u.

weigh.title: Weigh and add up
weigh.idea: Each triangle is multiplied by the weight of its criterion, and the triangles of a row are added up.
weigh.why: Important criteria count for more, and the uncertainty of every rating is carried along to the sum.

degrees.title: Compare with both references
degrees.idea: Each fuzzy sum is divided by the fuzzy sum of the anti-ideal row (K̃⁻) and of the ideal row (K̃⁺).
degrees.why: In a fuzzy division l is divided by u, m by m and u by l, so the result is still a valid triangle and keeps all of the uncertainty.

utility.title: A common yardstick
utility.idea: The two degrees of each alternative are added up (T̃), the largest sum D̃ becomes one number, and the utility functions are the degrees divided by it.
utility.why: Dividing by the same number puts the utility functions of every alternative on one scale.

crisp.title: One number per alternative
crisp.idea: Each fuzzy result becomes one number, and these numbers give the final utility.
crisp.why: Triangles cannot be ordered directly. One number per alternative makes the ranking possible.

ranking.title: Why this order?
ranking.idea: The alternatives are ordered by their final utility, highest first.
ranking.why: Below: the winner, the criteria that carried it, and where the runner-up is ahead or behind.

normalized-weight.how: The weight of {cell} is divided by the sum of all weights.
normalized-weight.meaning: {value} of the total weight goes to {cell}. The normalized weights add up to 1.

anti-ideal-benefit.how: {column} is a benefit criterion: the anti-ideal takes the smallest l, the smallest m and the smallest u of the column.
anti-ideal-benefit.meaning: {value} is the worst rating on {column}, number by number.

anti-ideal-cost.how: {column} is a cost criterion: the anti-ideal takes the largest l, the largest m and the largest u of the column.
anti-ideal-cost.meaning: {value} is the worst rating on {column}, number by number.

ideal-benefit.how: {column} is a benefit criterion: the ideal takes the largest l, the largest m and the largest u of the column.
ideal-benefit.meaning: {value} is the best rating on {column}, number by number.

ideal-cost.how: {column} is a cost criterion: the ideal takes the smallest l, the smallest m and the smallest u of the column.
ideal-cost.meaning: {value} is the best rating on {column}, number by number.

benefit.how: Each of the three numbers of {row} on {column} is divided by the upper value u of the ideal.
benefit.meaning: {value} is the rating of {row} on {column} as a share of the best. Numbers close to 1 are close to the ideal.

cost.how: For a cost criterion the lower value l of the ideal is divided by each number of {row}. l and u swap places, so the order l ≤ m ≤ u still holds.
cost.meaning: {value} is the rating of {row} on {column} as a share of the best. Numbers close to 1 are close to the ideal.

weighted.how: The fuzzy value of {row} on {column} is multiplied by the weight of {column}, number by number.
weighted.meaning: {value} is what {column} contributes to {row}, together with its uncertainty.

sum.how: The weighted fuzzy values in the row of {cell} are added up, number by number.
sum.meaning: {value} is the fuzzy overall performance of {cell}.

k-minus.how: The fuzzy sum of {row} is divided by the fuzzy sum of the anti-ideal row: l by u, m by m and u by l.
k-minus.meaning: {row} performs about {value} times as well as the worst possible alternative.

k-plus.how: The fuzzy sum of {row} is divided by the fuzzy sum of the ideal row, with the same fuzzy division.

t.how: The two fuzzy utility degrees of {cell} are added up, number by number.
t.meaning: {value} is T̃ of {cell}: both comparisons together.

d.how: D̃ takes the largest l, the largest m and the largest u among all T̃.
d.meaning: {value} is the largest combined degree: the yardstick of the next step.

df.how: D̃ is turned into one number (defuzzified).
df.meaning: Every fuzzy utility function is divided by {value}.

f-k-minus.how: The utility of {row} with respect to the anti-ideal: K̃⁺ divided by df_crisp. Note the crossover, as the authors define it.
f-k-minus.meaning: {value} is the fuzzy utility function f(K̃⁻) of {row}.

f-k-plus.how: The utility of {row} with respect to the ideal: K̃⁻ divided by df_crisp.
f-k-plus.meaning: {value} is the fuzzy utility function f(K̃⁺) of {row}.

defuzzify.how: The fuzzy value of {row} under {column} is turned into one number (defuzzified).
defuzzify.meaning: {value} is the number the final utility uses.

final-utility.how: The crisp K⁺ and K⁻ of {cell} are added up and divided by a term made from the two crisp utility functions.
final-utility.meaning: {value} is the final utility of {cell}. The alternative with the highest value ranks first.

data.title: The data
data.idea: CRITIC finds the weights from the data alone: nobody has to say which criterion matters more.
data.why: It looks at two things: how much a criterion separates the alternatives, and how much it says something the other criteria do not.

normalize.title: Scale to 0–1
normalize.idea: Every column is rescaled so that its worst value becomes 0 and its best value becomes 1.
normalize.why: Only then can columns with different units be compared. For a cost criterion the lowest value becomes 1.

contrast.title: How much does it separate?
contrast.idea: For each criterion: the mean, how far each value is from the mean, and the standard deviation σ.
contrast.why: If every alternative scores about the same on a criterion, it cannot help to choose between them. A large σ means strong contrast.

correlation.title: Does it repeat another criterion?
correlation.idea: The correlation r of every pair of criteria is calculated.
correlation.why: A correlation close to 1 means two criteria move together and say almost the same thing. Close to 0 or negative, they say different things.

information.title: How much new information?
information.idea: Conflict adds up 1 − r over all criteria, and the information content is C = σ × conflict.
information.why: A criterion carries a lot of information when it separates the alternatives well and disagrees with the other criteria.

weights.title: Information becomes weight
weights.idea: The weight of each criterion is its share of the total information.
weights.why: The weights add up to 1. The criterion with the most information gets the largest weight.

benefit.how: For the benefit criterion {column}: (value of {row} − worst value) ÷ (best value − worst value).
benefit.meaning: On {column}, {row} stands at {value} on the way from the worst value (0) to the best (1).

cost.how: For the cost criterion {column}, where the largest value is the worst: (worst value − value of {row}) ÷ (worst value − best value).
cost.meaning: On {column}, {row} stands at {value} on the way from the worst value (0) to the best (1).

mean.how: The normalized values of {cell} are added up and divided by the number of alternatives.
mean.meaning: {value} is the average of {cell}. The next step measures how far each value is from it.

deviation.how: The mean of {column} is subtracted from the normalized value of {row}.
deviation.meaning: On {column}, {row} is {value} away from the average. A negative value is below the average.

sigma.how: The squared deviations of {cell} are averaged, and the square root is taken.
sigma.meaning: {value} is the contrast of {cell}: the larger it is, the more the alternatives differ on this criterion.

pearson.how: The deviations of {row} and {column} are multiplied alternative by alternative, added up, and divided by n and by both standard deviations.
pearson.meaning: {value} is the correlation of {row} and {column}: close to 1 they move together, close to −1 in opposite directions.

conflict.how: For {cell}, 1 − r is added up over every criterion.
conflict.meaning: {value} is the conflict of {cell}: the less it correlates with the others, the larger it is.

information.how: The standard deviation of {cell} is multiplied by its conflict.
information.meaning: {value} is the information content C of {cell}.

weight.how: The information content of {cell} is divided by the total information of all criteria.

data.title: The data
data.idea: MEREC finds the weights from the data alone, by asking what happens when a criterion is left out.
data.why: A criterion whose removal changes the performance of the alternatives a lot is important.

normalize.title: Distance from the worst
normalize.idea: Every value is divided so that the worst value of its column becomes 1 and better values become smaller.
normalize.why: This is the reverse of most methods, on purpose: the logarithms of the next step grow as values move away from the worst, so a better performance gives a larger number.

performance.title: Overall performance
performance.idea: The overall performance S of each alternative is calculated from the logarithms of its values.
performance.why: |ln n| is 0 for the worst value and grows for better ones. S sums them up over all criteria.

removal.title: Leave one criterion out
removal.idea: S is calculated again for every alternative, each time without one criterion.
removal.why: Comparing with the full S shows how much each criterion contributes.

effects.title: Removal effect
effects.idea: The removal effect E of a criterion adds up how much S changes when the criterion is left out.
effects.why: The larger the change, the more the criterion matters for telling the alternatives apart.

weights.title: Effect becomes weight
weights.idea: The weight of each criterion is its share of the total removal effect.
weights.why: The weights add up to 1. The criterion with the largest effect gets the largest weight.

benefit.how: For the benefit criterion {column}: the smallest value of the column ÷ the value of {row}.
benefit.meaning: {value}: 1 would be the worst value on {column}. The smaller the number, the better {row} is.

cost.how: For the cost criterion {column}: the value of {row} ÷ the largest value of the column.
cost.meaning: {value}: 1 would be the worst value on {column}. The smaller the number, the better {row} is.

abs-ln.how: The absolute natural logarithm of the normalized value of {row} on {column}.
abs-ln.meaning: {value}: 0 stands for the worst value, larger numbers for values further from it.

overall.how: The absolute logarithms of {cell} are averaged over all criteria, 1 is added, and the natural logarithm is taken.
overall.meaning: {value} is the overall performance S of {cell} with every criterion.

removal.how: Like S of {row}, but without the term of {column}. The divisor stays the number of all criteria.
removal.meaning: {value} is the performance of {row} when {column} is left out.

effect.how: For {cell}, the difference |S′ − S| is added up over all alternatives.

weight.how: The removal effect of {cell} is divided by the sum of all effects.

order.title: Order of importance
order.idea: An expert lists the criteria from the most to the least important and says how much less important each one is than the one before.
order.why: This comparative importance s is a small number: the larger it is, the bigger the drop from the previous criterion. The first criterion has none; it is the reference.

coefficients.title: Coefficients
coefficients.idea: Each comparative importance s becomes a coefficient k = s + 1.
coefficients.why: The first criterion gets k = 1. A larger k means a bigger step down from the previous criterion.

chain.title: Step by step down the list
chain.idea: Going down the list, the value of each criterion is the value of the previous one divided by its coefficient.
chain.why: So importance falls step by step, exactly as much as the expert said.

weights.title: Weights that add up to 1
weights.idea: The values are divided by their sum.
weights.why: Only the proportions between the criteria matter. After this step the weights add up to 1.

first.how: {cell} is the most important criterion, so its coefficient is 1.
first.meaning: {value}: the reference the other criteria are compared with.

coefficient.how: 1 is added to the comparative importance of {cell}.
coefficient.meaning: {value}: the larger it is, the bigger the drop in importance from the previous criterion.

first.how: The first criterion starts the chain with 1.
first.meaning: {value}: the starting point of the chain.

recalculated.how: The value of the previous criterion is divided by the coefficient of {cell}.
recalculated.meaning: {value} is the importance of {cell} compared with the first criterion.

weight.how: The value of {cell} is divided by the sum of all values.

order.title: Order of importance
order.idea: An expert lists the criteria by importance and says in words how much less important each one is than the one before.
order.why: Words such as weakly less significant become triangular fuzzy numbers through the IMF SWARA scale. The first criterion has none; it is the reference.

coefficients.title: Coefficients
coefficients.idea: Each assessment s̃ becomes a fuzzy coefficient k̃ = s̃ + 1.
coefficients.why: The first criterion gets (1, 1, 1). A larger coefficient means a bigger step down from the previous criterion.

chain.title: Step by step down the list
chain.idea: Going down the list, each fuzzy value is the previous one divided by its coefficient, and then all of them are added up.
chain.why: Importance falls step by step. The fuzzy division (l by u, m by m, u by l) keeps the uncertainty of the words.

fuzzyWeights.title: Fuzzy weights
fuzzyWeights.idea: Each fuzzy value is divided by the fuzzy sum.
fuzzyWeights.why: This gives every criterion its share of the importance, still as a triangle.

weights.title: One number per criterion
weights.idea: Each fuzzy weight becomes one number, and the numbers are scaled so that they add up to 1.
weights.why: Other methods, such as MARCOS, need one weight per criterion.

first.how: {cell} is the most important criterion, so its coefficient is (1, 1, 1).
first.meaning: {value}: the reference the other criteria are compared with.

coefficient.how: 1 is added to each number of the assessment of {cell}.
coefficient.meaning: {value}: the larger it is, the bigger the drop in importance from the previous criterion.

first.how: The first criterion starts the chain with (1, 1, 1).
first.meaning: {value}: the starting point of the chain.

recalculated.how: The fuzzy value of the previous criterion is divided by the coefficient of {cell}: l by u, m by m and u by l.
recalculated.meaning: {value} is the importance of {cell} compared with the first criterion.

sum.how: The fuzzy values of all criteria are added up, number by number.
sum.meaning: {value} is the total the fuzzy weights are calculated from.

weight.how: The fuzzy value of {cell} is divided by the fuzzy sum.

defuzzify.how: The fuzzy weight of {cell} is turned into one number (defuzzified).
defuzzify.meaning: {value} is the crisp weight of {cell} before scaling. These numbers do not add up to exactly 1.

normalized.how: The crisp weight of {cell} is divided by the sum of all crisp weights.

why.title: Why not one number?
why.idea: People often cannot give an exact number, only a range: about 7.
why.why: A crisp number pretends to be certain. A fuzzy number keeps the range in the calculation.

triangle.title: Three numbers
triangle.idea: About 7 can be written with three numbers: the least it can be, the most likely value, and the most it can be.
triangle.why: Together they draw a triangle. Its height at a point shows how plausible that value is: full at the most likely value, zero outside the range.

scale.title: From words to triangles
scale.idea: A linguistic scale gives every word a triangle.
scale.why: Experts can answer in words, such as high or low, and Mateo calculates with the triangle of each word.

arithmetic.title: Calculating with triangles
arithmetic.idea: Two triangles are added by adding their l, their m and their u.
arithmetic.why: The uncertainty grows with every step: the sum is wider than both numbers. Other operations follow similar rules.

try.title: Try it yourself
try.idea: Drag the corners of two triangles and watch the result.
try.why: Every result below is calculated by Mateo's fuzzy arithmetic, the same one the methods use.

why.chart: The crisp number 7 and the fuzzy number about 7
why.meaning: The triangle says: certainly not below 5 or above 9, and most likely 7.

triangle.meaning: Writing {value} says: between the first and the last number, most likely the middle one. The numbers are always in order, l ≤ m ≤ u.

scale.meaning: When a rating such as High is entered, Mateo calculates with its triangle. The scales of a project are set up under Settings.

arithmetic.how: l + l, m + m, u + u:
arithmetic.single: To rank alternatives, a triangle is finally turned into one number. With the graded mean (l + 4m + u) / 6, {value} becomes {mean}.
arithmetic.meaning: Fuzzy methods carry the whole triangle through every step and only turn it into one number at the end.

operation.label: Operation
operation.scale: Multiply by a number  k · A

rule.add: The l, m and u values are added one by one.
rule.subtract: The lower value of A minus the upper value of B, the middle values subtracted, and the upper value of A minus the lower value of B.
rule.multiply: For positive numbers the l, m and u values are multiplied one by one.
rule.divide: For positive numbers: l of A divided by u of B, m by m, and u of A divided by l of B. B must not contain zero.
rule.scale: The l, m and u values are each multiplied by k.
rule.shift: The number k is added to l, m and u.
